newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac says will ensure French army gets resources.
newsitem.headline: Chirac says will ensure French army gets resources.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Sunday he would make sure that the armed forces, fearful of possible budget cuts by a new left-wing government, received the resources they needed.

The conservative president told a Defence Ministry reception on the eve of the Bastille Day military parade: "As head of the armed forces, I will take care that our forces continue to have the necessary resources both for their renovation and to maintain their capabilities and their training."

Chirac, who launched a landmark shift from conscription to all-professional armed forces last year, said he would review with the Socialist-led government what objectives had been met after the first year of a 1996 six-year military planning law.

"Today, we have made a good start...With the government, we are going to draw up a balance sheet of objectives achieved in this first year of implementation and the defence minister will send you the conclusions," he told senior commanders.
His comment appeared to be a warning shot across the bows of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who is looking for cost savings on defence.
Under the constitution, the president is commander-in-chief but has no control over the defence budget, which is adopted by the government and enacted by parliament.
Defence spending could become a source of friction in the current "cohabitation" between a president and government of opposite political parties.

Chirac made no mention of the government's decision to halt the privatisation of defence electronics giant Thomson-CSF, which he had launched. However he is expected to be asked about it in a television interview on Monday.

The previous centre-right government defeated in last month's parliamentary election had pledged to hold defence spending level for five years. But it froze 1.8 billion francs of the 1997 defence budget earlier this year as a precaution.
Senior army officers were worried by the appointment of a tough budget expert, Socialist Alain Richard, with no military expertise, as defence minister last month.
Richard confirmed that freeze this month and said he intended "to make progress in the relationship between public spending and efficiency".

Jospin has not yet set 1998 spending targets for the defence ministry, although he has sent written instructions to all other ministers, fuelling speculation he may seek substantial cuts, perhaps by delaying or scrapping costly weapons programmes.
He referred in a television interview on July 3 to a state Court of Auditors report which criticised the spiralling cost of armaments programmes.

Chirac said the modernisation of the armed forces was fully under way, citing as a symbol the fact that new Leclerc main battle tanks would take part for the first time in Monday's parade on the Champs-Elysees avenue.

The president paid tribute to the work of French troops both in the Vigipirate anti-terrorism security operation at home and on peacekeeping missions in Bosnia, Albania, Lebanon and Africa. Seventeen French soldiers have been killed on duty in the last year and about 180 wounded.
